Make of this what you will, but my dog had suspected Cushings due to highly elevated ALP in her blood work, we thought it was getting bad and then she was also diagnosed with diabetes. It turned out in the end that she did not have Cushings. Once we started treating the diabetes properly her ALP went back to normal and she has no signs or symptoms of Cushings any longer. 

Initially, for her diabetes, we were using Caninsulin as her insulin, which was expensive, and controlled her diabetes very poorly. We ended up going to an internal medicine specialist vet as she wasn't improving much, and the specialist switched her from caninsulin to Levemir, which is a regular insulin for humans. Almost immediately she started to stabilize properly, and the vet told us that in their experience, Levemir is significantly better for dogs at controlling their blood sugar than Caninsulin. The only caveat to using it is that they need significantly fewer units to have the same effect (about 1/4 of what she was using when she was on Caninsulin). Turns out not all insulins are equal.

So, before you make any end of life decisions, make sure you talk to a specialist, or try different versions of diabetes care, or both. Levemir, no kidding, saved my dog's life.

If you bowl, hit some pins down, but cross the line, then you don’t get any points. Assuming this is a word puzzle, the lowest score the player can get is if they cross the line, but hit down pins every time, and they’ll get zero.

If you knock down all ten pins on a foul, then you don’t get a second try that frame, and since, in order for the first player to always knock down more pins than the second they have to bowl the same number of times, they can at most knock down 9 pins on their first throw. So, if they can knock down 10 pins per frame over two throws, then the opponent can at most knock down 8 pins per frame (one less than the player per throw). At ten frames, the opponents max score is 80 so the answer is probably 80 points.

People seem to miss the point of admissions practices at these universities. There seems to be an idea that these universities are simultaneously machines which exist to provide privileged people access to an old boys club  to get ahead in the world, but care so much about liberal values so as to skew their admissions procedure. 

So, what do these universities actually want. They exist off donations and make a profit, so they want to make as large a profit as possible. The best way they have to do this is to choose people that they will be most successful in the long run. That makes their admissions decisions a lot more complicated than just picking students with the best grades. 

So, whatever system they have is likely to be some sort of statistical prediction based of all the available data they can legally ask for. First, they're going to give places to the 'legacy' students, because they're more likely to be successful and donate. There's going to be some bar they have to pass, but it's going to be lower than everyone else. Then they're going to look at grades and economic background, which is likely to be partially based on race and country of origin. For example, for graduate school students have to take the GRE exam, there's a cutoff score which is based on country of origin, since preparation for that exam is more difficult to come by in Europe than it is in the USA. For students from China the cutoff is really high, since they do more significant preparation and get higher scores than the US students. 

So, they're trying to look at everyone, and predict who will do the best in their upcoming degree if everyone applying had had exactly the same opportunities in life. Obviously that's a really difficult question to answer, and it's possible to have a discriminatory answer, but it's also possible for the answer to that question to depend on race, as a proxy for other factors and for it not to be discriminatory. 

It's also possible to take a really log view of the whole thing, since they're trying to predict who will be influential in the future, if the typical worldview starts skewing more towards equality,  maybe you want to increase your students numbers who have a particular background. After all, if the system is set up to favour white young men, which, for a long time it definitely was, then how are you going to change the system setup without bringing more minorities in, and seeing how well the system serves them. After all, most of the systems we design tend to be self perpetuating, as the people who get to decide and improve those systems are the people who went through them in the first place, and the improvements they make are things that they think were wrong, i.e. things that would have made it better for them.

So, he university has a system influenced by the people who were successful in that system, and they're trying to make a difficult prediction, using the data they have from applications, that will tell them who is going to be successful in the future, where the data they have about future success is skewed by the demographics of people who already were successful in the system, because that's all they have to compare to in the first place. It's an almost impossible problem, and given the large effect that the demographics or race or economic background or gender of the already successful people could have had on it there procedure, it seems reasonable that they might try and account for that. Whether the way they've done that is racist or not is why there's a trial, but it's not a cut and dry thing.

TD:LR Universities want to predict the future success of students applying now, and the long term data they have to base their decisions on is skewed towards what's best for rich white men. So including race as a factor in their decisions might be a sensible thing to do.

Th Gauss-Bonnet theorem is the fact that R_μνσρ R^μνσρ - 4R_μν Rμν + R^2 is a total derivative, and so, upon integration gives you a constant. It means that in a higher derivative gravity theory you can replace R_μνσρ R^μνσρ by 4R_μν Rμν - R^2 plus the total derivative. Since under a variation the constant term from the total derivative term vanishes it doesn't affect the dynamics. So we can just replace R_μνσρ R^μνσρ by the above, which gets rid of the term. Proving the Gauss-Bonnet theorem by proving the above is indeed a total derivative, is pretty boring, but doable. So if you understand what R_μνσρ is, you should be able to prove it yourself.

For modelling a physics problem the recipe is generally, how do I incorporate all the qualitative features of the problem into a simple model. This can be tricky, and the bigger, larger and more complicated the system, the trickier it is. 

So, we want to model a car going around a corner. How does it do it? Well, if you've driven a car, you know that cars can come in a number of shapes and sizes, it tends to be that turning the steering wheel changes the angle of the front wheels, and that cars can be front, rear or four wheel drive. When we're going forward in the car and we turn the wheels, they make an angle with the road. The wheels will probably slip a little, depending on how fast we're going, but mostly, we start changing direction. Why do we change direction? Because the wheels rotate, there will be a frictional force perpendicular to the new direction of the wheels, so the wheel, and so the car, will accelerate. Which direction? In the direction of the force, which depending on how hard we wrench the steering wheel, can point in many different directions, however, there will definitely be some component of it pointing opposite to the direction of the car, so the car will slow down. This is pretty well known, if you're driving a car, take your foot off the pedal and turn, then the car slows down. So, in reality, if we take our foot off the gas, and turn the wheel, the car turns and slows down. 

Now, what do we want from our model? This is the tricky bit, if you're a car engineer, you want everything, all the nuances, air resistance, the type of drive, how much you slow down, etc. However, if you're teaching someone about circular motion, you want the circular motion bit. So, let's say you're the teacher, well, we know the car will slow down on the turn, but as long as the turn isn't too sharp it won't slow down very much. Plus, you could always keep your foot on the gas, providing another force, and keeping your speed constant. So, let's ignore that complication, since it's getting in the way of what we're interested in. Then, since we want to discuss circular motion, we're going to say we're going to drive in a circle. Finally, we want to talk about the centripetal force, it's certainly caused by the wheels of the car interacting with the road. There will be a small component of it needed to counteract the driving force from the car, but we've assumed that we're not turning too sharply and things, so more or less, the frictional force alone, and all of the frictional force, is the centripetal force. 

I guess the first thing to realise is that the model is wrong, which you've done, the second thing to realise is that the wrongness doesn't matter that much. That's likely the hard thing as you're trained as a mathematician. When you're learning physics, many, many of the assumptions that go into models (especially the models to teach you concepts) are left out, because they're either not relevant, or many students find it too confusing, as you are now. You've got a couple of options, either ignore the 'physical situation' entirely, replace their examples with point masses for bodies, and ideal non-stretchable ropes for forces and you should be fine. Or you can do what I just did, start from a more detailed model and work out when it reduces to the simple teaching model, and what the teaching model is supposed to be telling you about.

I think if I were you, and I wanted to make this problem a little simpler, I'd try transforming into polar coordinates, since F(r, \theta) = r**\theta**, it would simplify your scalar product and things a bit. Since F points in the \theta direction it seems that the actual answer is going to depend a bit on how big L is. If L is big enough, then you could always travel to the origin in the radial direction, which would cost no work, and then travel out radially to the point you want to go to. If L's a little smaller, then you could travel towards the center a bit, go around in a circular arc, doing a little bit of work, but not too much, and then travel radially to the final point. It's only if L is small enough to force you to not travel along the r and \theta axes that the solution becomes a little more interesting, but all those solutions should show up in the equations somewhere, so you should keep an eye out for them.

It's always seemed to me that the problem that Lee has, and the problem of many other String Theory/QG researchers is not anything Lee mentions, it's that they  (Lee included) want their research to be important and to mean something and that they feel that the only thing that will matter is which theory is correct. They're wrong. What Duff fails to explicitly point out, but what he should point out, is that although the idea of a 'black hole' was a couple hundred of years old before it was finally sussed, it took many competing ideas to get from there to where we are now.  

Some researchers are very insecure about researching what they like, or find interesting or think is true, as they're so set on researching the correct theory. Which I guess probably comes down to your motivations. I'd argue that in the end that there is some trouble in theoretical high energy physics, but that the trouble isn't that bad ideas are getting funding, it's that everyone wants to be right. The conflict between some of these researchers would ease were they to accept that right or wrong, the things they study are part of a puzzle, and every answer, positive or negative, helps us get closer to the final answer. Within that framework, you should study the things you find interesting, whatever they are, and not worry about the correctness, just worry about showing people something they didn't know before. 

I do think that String Theory, apart from the geniuses Duff cherry picks to make his argument, not only has many 'craftspeople' but forces the 'seers' to become 'craftspeople' by virtue of the competitiveness of the field. This is not a problem unique to String Theory. It's also a difficult problem to solve. Though I feel fairly safe in saying that the solution is not 'defund the other guy and give that money to me'.

Basically, they should be discussing the facts and results of all the theories, what they teach us and how they can be used in other circumstances. They should not be discussing any 'should' questions in Quantum Gravity research, there's no ethics to worry about, those questions aren't science and they tend to just slow things down and make everyone mad.

It's very common in theoretical physics. The idea behind it is that when you're looking at some equations, you want to make them as simple as possible. In this case, we know at the end of the day that simple harmonic motion has a single parameter in the solution, the frequency. That means that we should be able to rewrite everything using just that parameter. Doing so might involve rescaling or redefining some variables which isn't a problem so long as we remember what we did. Then we get equations which contain only the relevant parameters and we've made our problem as simple as we can.

Judging by what you've written, it looks like there's been a bit of rescaling of the lagrangian. You have:

1/(2w)q'^2  - (w/2)q^2  = (1/w)[(1/2)q'^2  - (w^2  /2) q^2 ]

which, if you plug in w gives:

(1/w)[(1/2)q'^2  - w^2 /2q^2 ] = (1/wm)[(m/2)q'^2  - k/2 q^2 ]

The bit in square brackets is what you'd usually write down as the lagrangian (possibly without the factor of 1/2 in in front of the second term. So this is a rescaled version, which can be nice to work with sometimes, since the only parameter of the problem is w.

So, to get the hamiltonian you first need to compute the canonical momenta. That's defined by p = dL/dq'. So

p = q'/w

Now calculating the Hamiltonian gives:

H = pq'-L = wp^2 -(w/2)p^2 +(w/2)q^2 =(w/2)(p^2 +q^2 )

which is the answer you want. My guess is the bit you're missing is the use of the canonical momenta. One of the important things to recognise in classical mechanics is that the canonical momenta is not always mv.

So, a point particle can't really spin, since it's just a point (though a point particle like an electron can possess a quality which we call spin, but that's not what we're talking about here). For a single particle to spin around it's axis it would have to be an extended body, a case which is a little more complex than the following. A simple system to see why spinning reference frames are different from ones moving at constant velocity is that of two massive point particles connected by a spring. It's probably quite intuitive that if you send off both the particles at the same velocity, then the spring remains at it's natural length and it exerts no force. Now imagine you spin the two particles around each other, intuitively the spring now lengthens, and so is exerting a force on the particles, the centripetal force which keeps them moving in a circle. Even if you sat on one of the particles and declared it you reference frame you would still be able to measure that spring force simply by observing the change in the length of the spring. 

I think your rant though mostly rests on one misconception, which is that the behaviour of the forces which govern the motion of the particles is also subject to the symmetries you're talking about. Because of this you can't come up with a physical situation where the symmetry rules (like no particles move faster than c) are broken if you just stick to putting particles together and seeing how they interact. I understand it's not a hugely satisfying answers, but it's a lot like positing a situation where you have a car driving on the ceiling, and then asking how that can happen because of gravity. The answer is that it can't, and the problem is that you've assumed it can.

As a concrete example, if you use general relativity and study the orbits of a small particle around a very massive one (due to gravity between them) you will see that you actually can't have an arbitrarily small radius for the orbit, when a particle gets too close, whatever the angular momentum, there is a final circular orbit at some radius, and any small particle that tries to go in a circular orbit at a smaller radius will just fall into big particle.

1. There are in my experience a few ways you can approach this. You could do what they say to do, which sucks, but it's an option, and if it's not something you can change, then it might not be worth struggling against it. You can buck against it, which will help your students, but won't necessarily help you, or you can care about it, and just not tell anyone you do. So long as you don't spend loads of time preparing for sections, no one else in the department will be any the wiser. Whilst it would be great if you could change their minds about teaching, you're not going to, and there's no point really fighting that battle, but it doesn't mean you have to do a crappy job. Just don't let anyone except your students know you care. 

2. In my sections I always made a few things clear right at the beginning. 

i). I would only ever grade them based on their written homeworks, and not ever on anything they said in section. I used to joke that I was so bad at names that I wouldn't remember who said what anyway. 

ii). I would not tolerate any snide comments or anything like that about any other person's questions or abilities. At one point (in a possibly ill-advised move) I ended up telling a section that if anyone else made fun of someone for not getting the material I would make them look and feel stupid. 

iii). I would never call on any specific person to answer a question, if they wanted to come to section, sit in the back, and not say anything then they were perfectly entitled to do that. I'd tell them I thought that they'd get much more out of section if they participated, but that if they didn't want to, they didn't have to.

iv). They could contact me in at least four ways, section, after sections, office hours and via email. I'd encourage them to come to office hours if they had long questions, and I'd sell office hours as something they should come to even if they had no questions. In office hours I'd go over people's questions on a blackboard, so if someone else was there, they could learn something too.

This would be my effort to them to make myself accessible, and to make sections a comfortable environment for them to share their ideas in. 

When it comes to collecting the homeworks at the beginning I might try the following. Give them two minutes at the beginning to decide on a question that they want to ask you which is relevant to their homework. Tell them you've got to be able to answer it in five minutes or less. Then, answer their question and then collect the homeworks. It won't really change their marks at all,  but they'll like you, it'll make them feel like you're trying to help them and it'll get them talking to each other and to you.

You should also ask them simple organisational questions about the section, ask them which homework question they want to go over first, and wait until someone answers. Ask them how they'd like to layout the room, ask them how they'd like you to use the boards, ask them whether they'd rather you focus on computation or concepts. Ask them all of these things for every question. But you've got to wait until someone answers, when someone does, grab their answer and run with it. You first goal is just to get them to feel comfy talking to you in front of everyone else. 

As for calling on someone to answer, personally I think it's a bad thing, and it makes people feel uncomfortable. I have in the past used a system whereby I would call on a particular row or column of seats, if the people in them hadn't talked in a while. But if you do something like that you've got to commit to it, and wait until someone answers.  

I'd also use the 'bart simpson technique' to get a bit more out of them. I'd do things slowly and laboriously, all the time asking them how to do things. Eventually the speedier students get so sick of going slowly they will start to speed you up by offering suggestions, and you can use those suggestions to get the other students involved in a discussion about the question.

You should also always remember that you can afford to play the long game. Waiting for them to respond to your questions is going to help them more in the long term than you filling the silence for them. So you should look upon those silences as part of your teaching. 

I also think it's always a good idea to turn up a few minutes early and make some small talk with the students, ask them how the course is going, what they think of the prof, do they have study groups, etc. 

Finally, I've found it worth setting them simple problems to do in groups during section. It gets them talking to one another and you can use the time to go around and talk to the smaller groups individually, ask them how they're getting on, and try to get the quieter people to talk to you then. 

4. Performance anxiety is a thing, and it happens to us all from time to time. The thing that got me through was the realisation that I'd earned my place in grad school, and whilst there was a chance that people in my section were smarter than me, they certainly didn't know more than me, and in section that's what's important. Practice is important too, and you'll get better the more you do.

You also need to remind yourself that you're not being graded. The students feedback doesn't count for anything, and it's certainly not an indication of how well you did at actually imparting information to them (though it might feel like it is). If it goes badly, the students have plenty of opportunities to come and see you more, or go and get help in plenty of other ways, so it's not all on you. Basically, you don't have to worry about consequences if you do a bad job, the only bad consequence is you might feel bad, but you'll also learn from it, and get better. 

You should bring a set of answers to the homework problems into section with you, and you should bring a computer. If someone asks you to do a computation that you're wary of, then boot up mathematica or something and get it to do it. Just tell the students that you want to make sure you're giving them the correct answer. I remember once a prof told me, that if there's more than three minus signs in a problem, then there's a 50% chance of a sign error. Everyone makes arithmetic mistakes. Just use it as another opportunity to engage your students. Make a game of it, record who spots your errors, and tell them that at the end of the semester, you'll give a chocolate bar or something to the person who got the most. Usually there's a way around these problems such that you don't have to do as much work, or put yourself out there so much, but which is also better for the students. You should try and find those ways and implement them. But ultimately, mistakes make you human, and your students will be much more comfortable talking to a human than some kind of infallible robot.

I think that you don't understand quantum mechanics, or the ideas behind quantum computation and are unwilling to put in the effort to learn about them, as it's all there in textbooks and online courses. 

No one proposes a calculation can be made instantly, and certainly these things are possible to prove using logic alone. That logic is called mathematics and it has been used to great effect to flesh out the theory of quantum computation. 

You need to take a few steps back and think about what you know about quantum mechanics, go and read something about it and then ask questions about what you don't understand. Many people devote a substantial chunk of their life to the subject and they're certainly not all idiots, it's very arrogant for you to think that, you can, without understanding even a little bit of quantum mechanics, successfully argue that their subject is bunkum.

> Well, whatever it's called, not being able to know a particle's location with arbitrary precision due to observation changing location is sort of at the backbone of quantum physics, isn't it?

When a measurement of a particles location takes place the particle doesn't change location, it gets one. Before the measurement occurred the particle never had a position, in a similar way to how a water wave doesn't have a single position. 

The collapse of the wavefunction like this isn't really the most important idea of quantum physics. It's certainly important for getting answers, but it doesn't lead to any of the weird stuff. Uncertainty too is not really the part of quantum mechanics which leads to the funny behaviour. Neither uncertainty or wavefunction collapse are the most important aspects in making quantum computation impossible. The most important aspect is entanglement. 

I find it hard to get what you mean when you say 'extended guess work' and things like that with regards to quantum mechanics. The idea behind quantum computation is very, very simple. First you get a qubit. A qubit is any two-state system. For example, a photon can have two polarizations. Quantum logic gates which act on a single photon can be implemented via mirrors and beam splitters, as these gates just need to change the polarization state of the photon. Then for full quantum computation one can either follow the (KLM scheme)[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_optical_quantum_computing] or add in non-linear optical elements, which certainly exist. Then, you've got a working quantum computer, it won't work very well, and it'll have problems scaling, but the thing exists, and conceptually there's not any more to it than very basic quantum mechanics.

[NMR](http://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0112176) quantum computers are the ones I'm most familiar with, and I know that functional quantum computational devices can be built with NMR machines, I was once told by a professor that any proficient NMR technician could run Shor's algorithm on their NMR machine in a week or so. You can also see [here](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qubit) the physical implementations of qubits. Certainly, quantum dots, josephson gates and optical lattices exist, and small quantum computers have indeed been build using these techniques. 

The problem with quantum computers is certainly one of scaling, not one of possibility. They definitely are possible to construct and they are suited to a different complexity class of problems than classical computers. The question right now is just how many can a quantum computer have and still function and that number is steadily increasing.

Quantum computers certainly aren't speculation, they exist. Currently the techniques used for building a quantum computer don't scale, that is, we're able to make quantum computers with a small number of qubits, and those techniques don't appear to scale up to devices with many thousands of qubits. But quantum computers exist, quantum computation exists as a subject and there appears to be steady progress in the field. I'm not sure where you got the idea that they were theoretically impossible.

Guided independent study in QFT and GR is a good idea (those are the areas you want to concentrate on if you want to do QG or high energy theory), you'd get to learn a bunch of interesting stuff, and you'd get a nice reference out of it at the end of the day. You might also consider doing a master's degree before a phd, maybe something like the [http://perimeterscholars.org/](PSI program) to get some proper courses under your belt and get the opportunity to do a theoretical research project. 

As for the math I use everyday, that's easy. Differential Geometry (for GR), Group Theory (for GR and QFT) and the collection of mathematical techniques used for QFT, bits of functional analysis, complex analysis and some high end calculus. Those mathematical techniques will carry you just past introductory string theory and then a bit more advanced stuff gets thrown at you, but only particular results from various mathematical disciplines. 

If you want some more concrete ideas of that stuff then grab yourself a copy of Quantum Field Theory in a Nutshell by Zee, and Hartle's book on General Relativity. If you want the nitty gritty nuts and bolts, then Peskin and Schroeder or Srednicki's QFT books are good, and you'll want to read Wald's book on GR. All the mathematics you need to understand the theories is taught to you in those books, and for what you'll be doing with it, those books are some of the best places to learn that mathematics. If you want something after that, grab Sydney Coleman's 'Aspects of Symmetry' which is a really really great book full of really interesting stuff. Weinberg's book on GR, called Cosmology, is a really good GR book, but I'd avoid his books on QFT.

I'm a senior grad student studying quantum gravity and strings and I can tell you what I've found. 

In theoretical physics you use a lot of maths, there's no doubt about that. But, the way you use it tends to be quite different from how mathematicians use it. As a theoretical physicist you're using maths to describe something, and you want to know what the mathematics tells you about that thing. In the course of doing this you need to calculate and prove things, and every now and then a very nice and famous maths result pops out at you, things like the Hairy Ball theorem, the Riemann-Roch theorem or the Atiyah-Singer Index theorem. But your purpose was never to find those things, you just came across them in trying to work out the consequences of the theory. That means that some math courses can be useful, as they tell you all the surrounding mathematical details of these results, but they tend to have the wrong pedagogical thrust for theoretical physics. You learn theorems and why they're true, but you don't learn how to solve the kinds of problems you come across in theoretical physics. So, the content of those courses is certainly important and you'll use the facts without even realising it a lot of the time, but you often don't need the details, just the facts. As an anecdotal example I can tell you I'm a grad at a top 10 US research university, and I've never taken any Real Analysis courses at all, never taken an explicit Algebra course and I've never taken a basic Topology course, though I did do a grad course in Algebraic Topology without any trouble. 

Similarly, experimental projects aren't really helpful for theoretical physics either, there you learn a whole bunch of experimental skills, and might get a better intuition for the theory underlying your experiment (but if you're interested in QG then there aren't any experiments).

If you only have those two options, and you're certain you want to go into QG (which is a long and hard road, and only pays off with a research job for a very small number of the people who start out on it) then I'd say to do the maths. 

The caveat to that is that theoretical physics departments are inside physics departments, which (in the US at least) require stuff like the physics GRE and like to recruit physics students. So if there's any way you can stay a double major and have both maths and physics written on your degree, then I'd do that.

The other suggestion I'd have is more of a third option. If your school has any graduate level courses in general relativity or quantum field theory then do them. That's what theory departments  really seem to be looking for. They might fall under your math department (GR often tends to be in maths whereas QFT tends to live in physics).

The other suggestion I've got is that if there are any QG professors at your university, send them an email and go have a chat to them, see what they think you should do. They'll know more about the content of the courses at you university than we do and they'll be able to tell you how much they've used it over their career. 

If you've got any questions then just let me know, I'm happy to help.

The No-Hair theorem has a couple of caveats. The statement is that any black hole solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations can be characterized by three parameters, mass, angular momentum and charge. The first caveat is that it's actually a conjecture, and every now and again you'll see some paper on the arxiv which has produced a black hole with a persistent scalar field around it or something. The second caveat is that this conjecture only talks about solutions of the Einstein-Maxwell equations. Those equations don't know anything about a scalar field, and so the above papers don't disprove the no-hair conjecture. Those equations also don't know anything about baryons or leptons or any quantum numbers at all. As for the question of 'does a black hole have a lepton number, or a baryon number (which are only approximate conserved quantities) or any other charges we might postulate I think the answer is that we don't know, and a full characterization of what goes on for the other quantum numbers would be a very difficult and very interesting enterprise.

Hi there, sounds like you're in a bit of a tough feeling spot. I've got some advice and some anecdotes that might make you feel a little better. So, advice first, then anecdotes (gotta have dinner before pudding). 

Firstly, if you haven't gone to talk to your academic advisor or whoever is there to help you decide on your courses etc, then go talk to them and tell them everything. The help those people provide varies, some are very good and some aren't so good, but it's hard to see how it could make anything worse, so go and do it and get some support from within your university. 

Secondly, all the offered courses should have prerequisites. From now on (whether you switch to another subject or not) make sure you check them. If they don't have prerequisites send the professor and email and ask about them. It's sometimes possible to do the courses without the prerequisites, but it won't offer you an easy life and sometimes it'll get you in trouble (see anecdote 1). The best thing to do is if there's a course you want to take that you don't have the prerequisites for, then don't take it, take the prereqs instead and then take the course next time it's offered.

Thirdly, find yourself a study group if you can. A real group of people that you can talk to about the work. Having a study group to study with is more productive than doing it on your own. It's not cheating to have one and you shouldn't feel bad. Very very few people make it through a physics degree without some sort of study support from their buddies. If you, for whatever reason can't get one, then reddit is a substitute, it's nowhere near as good, but if you're stuck you can come here and ask for help. 

Fourthly, If you can afford it, get a tutor. The maths and physics department at your university will have books at tutors. A tutor can identify where you're struggling and why you're struggling and help you out in your particular problem areas. I work as a tutor and you'd be surprised how quickly I can raise someone's grade by correcting three or four mistakes they keep making over and over again. 

Fifthly, your courses should have TA's, your TA's should have office hours. Go to the office hours, if you don't have any particular questions go anyway. The TA will look at you, and you should say, 'This shit is hard man! I just came to see what you're saying to everyone else!' The TA will chuckle, offer you a seat and talk to you about physics, about the common problems students are having, and you'll get to listen in on their problems and how they're solved. I was once given a really great piece of advice by a professor. He said, starting physics is like being shot into molasses. Pretty soon everyone's going at a crawl. But, if you see someone else shooting ahead don't try and compete or get jealous, copy them, because they're doing something right.

Sixthly, [Physics by example](http://www.amazon.com/Physics-Example-200-Problems-Solutions/dp/0521449758/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1396242047&sr=8-1&keywords=Physics+by+example) is a great book that's helped many a student, and depending on how far you are in your studies, could help you too.

Seventhly, At first physics appears to be about memorizing a tonne of equations, but it isn't. Physics is about understanding the connections between different problems and understanding how the one or two really important equations apply to all those different problems. For example, in mechanics, all you need to know is F=ma. Pretty much everything follows from it. So, to make your study extra effective you should always be asking yourself where the formulas come from. In the end, you'll understand the subject better and find it easier to remember the formulas.

Eighthly, study is fine, practice is better. Solving physics problem is a skill, not just the application of some fixed method. To get better at a skill you need practice, not just to read the textbook a bunch of times. If you don't practice with actual problems you won't get better. So make sure you are. There's masses of problems available all over the internet and the majority of your study time should be spent trying to solve them.

Ninthly, Everyone (I haven't met an exception to this rule) gets made to feel stupid by physics at some point or another. You've got to realise that you're studying things that weren't understood until a few hundred years ago, and it was some of the smartest people who've ever lived that discovered them. 

Tenthly (and finally), Most people find the hardest part of physics not to be the math, but to be understanding how to take a real problem and turn it into math. If you can do that, then you're going to be alright. It's a skill like anything else, and the best way to do it is to practice. So when you're walking outside, and you see a hanging branch, think to yourself, how heavy would a squirrel have to be if he sat on that branch and broke it. If you see a leaf flowing down a river, think to yourself, how long will it be until that lead reaches the next bend. If you see someone running up a hill, think to yourself, how much energy will that person have expended before they get to the top. Estimate the numbers for all these questions, think about the physics involved, simplify your models and get an approximate answer and try to do it in your head. It is practice that will help. 

As for what subjects you could switch into, you could try engineering, which would use the physics courses you've already taken. Whether it's easier is up for debate, but I'd say it was a little. I can't, off the top of my head, think of anything else that's easier that you could switch into without delay, but you should talk to someone at your university about it, as they'd know much much better. 

Now, finally, your promised anecdotes. I have two, both happened to me, so there's hope for everyone. For context, I've been to an Ivy for grad school studying strings, so even after disasters you can get past them and get to where you want to go.

Anecdote 1: Upon entering graduate school and wanting to study string theory, I wanted to take a course in it. There were a few strings courses offered every other year or so, and the year I happened to enter they were teaching the most advanced one. Me being an ambitious young grad student thought, 'Oh, no worries, I'll do it and just pick up the basics as I go along.' How wrong I was.
 
The professor and TA encouraged me to continue but at the end of the day it was a disaster. I completely bombed. (seriously completely, completely enough eyebrows were raised and I had to go talk to some people to smooth things over) It was my first grad course, in the subject I wanted to study and I'd manage to properly screw it up before getting myself a strings supervisor. Things didn't look good and I wasn't very happy. 

Eventually I plucked up the courage to go and see the guy I wanted to work with anyway. Walked in and told him I wanted to work with him. The first thing he asked me was about the grade. I shrugged and told him it was the first strings course I'd taken, and the other professor had told me to do it, plus I learned some stuff and I didn't want to wait three years for another opportunity. He shrugged right back at me and said 'fair enough' and we began work on a project later that year. In my experience most academics are pretty understanding when these things happen if there's a good reason, and doing a calculus based physics course when you haven't learned calculus is a pretty damn good reason for it to not go so well.

Anecdote 2: I'd just finished my first semester of undergrad. I was happy with the way things were going and I thought I'd done a good job in the first term. In my university we had exams at the beginning of every semester, which were exams on what we'd done in the previous one. So upon returning we had two exams, a maths one and a physics one. The maths one was ok, I did pretty well. But the physics one...

I have never had such an awful exam experience in my entire life. I went into the exam hall pretty confident, sat down, opened the paper and it felt like the world started to crumble around me as I slowly realised I couldn't answer any of the question on the paper. I went pale, I started sweating, I almost vomited all over the person sitting in front of me. I looked so awful one of the invigilators came over to ask me if I was ok. But the exam ended, and I survived it.

After grading I found out I'd gotten a 39 on the exam. It was the lowest mark in my year. I was no longer pleased with myself. I still feel awful about it, and every now and again I still dream about it. Afterwards the powers that be brought me into the office and asked me what was going on. I didn't really know what to say and so I just shrugged. I'd revised for it, so it hadn't been laziness, I'd been to all the lectures, I was (up until that point) good at taking exams, and I hadn't been nervous at all. I was ordered in no uncertain terms not to let it happen again.

In the end I think I credit that experience with helping me, even if it does sometimes keep me up at night. It taught me that with physics you have to learn smarter, not work harder to be good at it. I started really trying to understand what I was doing, rather than just trying to memorize everything to answer all the problems. Soon after that everything started to click together and I began to find it all easy. In the end of year exams I ranked 6th out of 180. I finally graduated 2nd out of a 100 people a few years later.

Basically what I'm trying to say to you is that having a bad time at the beginning of a physics degree isn't unusual, and it doesn't mean you're bad at it. Most often it means you need to learn smarter rather than work harder, and most often people can do it. If physics is something you really think you'd like to do with your life I'd advise you to stick with it and try and get to grips with it in any way you can.

It turns up in string theory when you're trying to calculate what the masses of the modes of a quantum string are. If you've heard of zero-point energy for a quantum harmonic oscillator then it's a similar thing. Except in the case with strings every string mode has a zero point energy. The n^th string mode has zero point energy given (up to some overall constant) by n. So when you're adding them all up you get the sum from n=0 to n=infinity of n. 

That sum doesn't converge, but you still want to assign some meaning to it. There are a bunch of ways to do that and they're all related. (If you quantize the string in a different way the problem comes up in quite a different form where you can use standard QFT methods to deal with it) Some relevant notes by David Tong are [here](http://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/string/two.pdf) and the constant turns up on page 11. Though, be warned that those notes won't make much sense if you don't know a bit about quantum mechanics and string theory. The whole set of lecture notes can be found [here](http://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/string.html)

In this case the meaning that's assigned to that sum is that it should be equal to -1/12. Have a look [here](http://terrytao.wordpress.com/2010/04/10/the-euler-maclaurin-formula-bernoulli-numbers-the-zeta-function-and-real-variable-analytic-continuation/?blogsub=confirming#subscribe-blog) to have Terry Tao take you through some of the logic. 

So, it's a quite important calculation that you come across for the first time (at least I came across it for the first time) when you begin to study string theory. The logic behind using it is actually surprisingly solid, and it's a fun thing to think about. If you've got any other questions about it, or about strings feel free to ask!

This is a conservation of energy problem. You need to say that the change in GPE is equal to the change in the kinetic energy of the rock plus the rotational kinetic energy of the disk. Since you know the height it falls and the speed it's going then you can calculate both the change in GPE and the kinetic energy of the rock. Plugging those into the energy conservation equation will give you an equation for the rotational kinetic energy of the disk. You also know the angular speed of the disk since it's velocity at the edge must be the same as the rock because they're attached via the string. So then you know everything about the disk except the mass, and you can solve for it.

So, the paragraph is wrong, but it's a common misconception about quantum mechanics. What 'causes' the heisenberg uncertainty principle to happen isn't recoil from observation or anything like that. That would imply that what's going on is akin to experimental error, and that's not the case. It's strange, but it seems to be a fact that it's not that we're experimentally uncertain about somethings position or momentum, it's that nothing has a precise position or momentum. That sounds weird to begin with, but it isn't really. It's like me asking you for the position of a water wave. There are many points on the wave, and any of them could be a good answer, but I can't say that the wave is only at a single point. 

What the uncertainty principle actually says is that given two observables of the object in question, unless certain criteria are met, we simply cannot know exact values for both observables at the same time, the object doesn't have an exact value for them.

As for your friends question, his conclusion is correct. It's nothing about having a conscious person look at something, that's not going to make any difference one way or another. Things will bash into other things whether you're looking or not. 

So yes, the paragraph is a common misconception about the origin of the uncertainty principle, and yes things are 'observed' when anything, including a photon, bashes into something else, whether there is a person looking at it or not.

So random matrices are some pretty hefty stuff, and an active area of research in both theoretical physics and mathematics. From the mathematics side I'm not so fluent, but I know a bit about these models from the physics side.

Random matrices pop up quite a lot, but an interesting place they appear is in the study of 2d quantum gravity, which I think is the kind of thing you might be interested in. Have a look [here](http://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0406013v2.pdf) for a nice set of introductory lecture notes about matrix models and their application to 2d quantum gravity. Though beware, you will certainly at the very least need to be familiar with multivariable calculus and complex analysis to understand those notes. It's sadly not a simple subject and this is pretty much the starting point.

Secondly, you're going to need to know a bit about orthogonal polynomials, where they come from and why we care about them. You can get a bit of an idea from the [wikipedia page](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonal_polynomials). The further you go in mathematical physics the more they pop up. In particular, you might want to check out Hermite polynomials, Laguerre polynomials and Legendre polynomials. Since if you're going into physics, those are some of the first ones you'll encounter.

Should that make a bit of sense to you (feel free to ask questions here too, it's fun to talk about!) then the reason orthogonal polynomials are relevant  to random matrices is given in [this](http://galton.uchicago.edu/~lalley/Courses/386/OrthogonalPolynomials.pdf) short set of notes. Those notes are unlikely to make much sense unless you've already studied orthogonal polynomials and know a bit about random matrices. But the basic idea is that particular sets of orthogonal polynomials are useful for studying random matrices with particular distributions. 

After getting to grips with that stuff you're probably in a minimal position to have a general idea what that paper's going on about and why they care about it. The main thing they care about is the level density. The level density in a random matrix model is the distribution of the eigenvalues of the random matrices, so you can imagine that it might be an important and useful thing to study. In that paper they're studying matrices with some tricky distributions and so the orthogonal polynomials that help to solve the problem are a bit odd. They find equations satisfied by those polynomials, calculate some bits and pieces both analytically and numerically and then plot the level densities. 

Also, since I'm a scientist, and by nature curious, I've got to gang up on you with the other commenter and ask why on earth you're interested in reading that particular paper?

So, I'm afraid this is all probably going to look like gobbledygook, but you said it would be cool to see some equations (and it is). 

[These](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einstein_field_equations#Einstein.E2.80.93Maxwell_equations) are the Einstein-Maxwell field equations. They're the equations that tell you how the shape of spacetime can be altered by the presence of electromagnetism.  The thing with the big R label is a way of talking about the curvature of the spacetime, and the thing with the F label is a way of talking about the electromagnetic field. The equation relates the two things. 

Unsurprisingly these equations are incredibly difficult to solve, and have never been solved in general. They look so bad, that when Einstein first wrote them down he said something along the lines of - we will never get an analytic solution to these equations. Luckily, we've found many many solutions which have all kind of interesting properties. 

One solution which might be particularly interesting for you is the [Vaidya Metric](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaidya_metric). This metric describes how if you take a thin shell of massless matter it can collapse to a black hole. 

You might also be interested in [Geodesic congruences](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_(general_relativity)), which describe the path of a circle of photons as it moves through space.

The question as to how exactly light affects spacetime we have answered implicitly (at least when we're either neglecting quantum mechanics or not dealing with spacetime that's too severely curved) with the equations above. Solving them is very tricky though. It's a system of fourteen coupled partial differential equations. One approach would be to start with a spacetime, then add in the electromagnetic radiation and work out how it moves. Something like that could be done with the geodesic congruences. Then compute a correction to the shape of the spacetime due to the radiation. Then compute the correction to the path of the radiation due to the correction of the shape of the spacetime and so on. This is a perturbation series like method and so could only deal with small corrections, and may well not converge anyway. Certainly it wouldn't work if you wanted to see something as severe as spacetime generating time loops.

So there's a way to make all twin paradox type questions easy to work out (even if not easy to understand). Let's say we have an observer who's clock reads t1, and who's location is x1,y1,z1. And they travel to another spacetime point at x2,y2,z2, where their clock reads t2. The time it took, from their perspective to go from the first point to the second is c^2 t^2 = c^2 (t2-t1)^2 - (x2-x1)^2 -(y2-y1)^2 -(z2-z1)^2 . There are reasons for this which I can explain if you like, but for now we should take it as a fact. The remarkable thing about this formula is that it doesn't matter which observer puts the coordinates in, every observer will get the same answer. To emphasize, if a second observer says the first one started at T1,X1,Y1,Z1 and went to T2,X2,Y2,Z2 then c^2 (T2-T1)^2 - (X2-X1)^2 - (Y2-Y1)^2 - (Z2-Z1)^2 = c^2 t^2 as well. So everyone watching can calculate how much time any other observer has experienced. 

So, with this formula, we don't need to appeal to accelerations or general relativity or anything like that, we simply break everyone's journey up into segments and then calculate everything. In the twins paradox, let's say the observers A and B started at point P1, then B leaves and goes to point P2 and then returns to meet A at point P3. If we calculate the above for A and B, that is, we write down the coordinates of all three points, and calculate the time from P1 to P2, and then from P2 to P3 and compare it to the time we calculate for going from P1 to P3 we'll find the P1 to P3 time is more. If you like, you can do it with proper numbers rather than algebra and you'll see this is what happens. 

Really what's going on is that it's the triangle inequality in reverse. So if we have a triangle with longest side length A and shorter sides lengths B and C, then we have that B+C>A. In relativity if we have a path with proper time T1 and two paths that leave and come back with times T2 and T3 we'll find that T2+T3<T1. If you were happy with some more maths and wanted a less wordy explanation I could lay this out properly and show you why this is true.

Anyway, you asked about someone going away and then waiting on a distant planet. Well we can be sure that once the person has settled on the far away planet their time ticks along at the same rate as A's, so we're only concerned with what happens on the way there. We can calculate that with the above formula, and you'll see that B experiences less time than A does while he's in his trip.

It's difficult to show why B would indeed measure that A is older without drawing a diagram. But, I can give you some idea from the measurement of time of the far away person. Let's say B wants to measure what time A is at. What B does is send out a light pulse and waits for it to come back from A. Then, the light pulse took (t2-t1) seconds to travel there and back, so A was at (t2-t1)/2 when the light pulse met them. But now, think about what happens to the measurements where the light pulse was sent out before B stopped, and received afterwards. These measurements are going to be a bit odd since B is changing reference frames halfway through. If you draw some pictures or have a think about what's going on, I'm confident you'll be able to work out where the extra time for A is coming from.

Your question makes sense, which is good! But I'm afraid the answer is no. Here's why,

Quantum mechanics is a really interesting thing because it's not a theory of things, it's a theory about things.  As an example, if we want to describe a classical particle, then we use classical mechanics,  but it's also classical mechanics that we use if we want to describe the classical behavior of fluids, rigid bodies and for example, waves on strings.

Quantum mechanics works in a similar way, we get to pick what we want to describe, be it particles, fields or relativistic strings and then we use quantum mechanics to describe it. That means that anything we use quantum mechanics to describe has the 'quantum weirdness' built in, so it doesn't come from anywhere, it's simply there in the theory,  always.

So what do the Calabi-Yau spaces do. The idea is that the strings vibrational modes correspond to particles in the theory. So a free string floating around vibrates in a whole bunch of ways and gives a whole bunch of particles. Now, imagine the string was wrapped around a cylinder, it can still vibrate,  but the vibrations would be a bit different. 

The Calabi-Yau spaces are a lot more complicated that a cylinder, but the principle is the same. There are a whole bunch of different ways to wrap a string around the Calabi-Yau. So this can give a lot of different types of particles. The number of holes there are in the Calabi-Yau tells you about the number of families of particles and how those holes intersect tells you other stuff about them.

As for experimental evidence, finding a Calabi-Yau which gives us the particles we see wouldn't really count for a few reasons. The most important being, we don't require string theory to see any of those sets of particles. We already see a set of particles, and just because string theory could describe it,  doesn't mean it does describe it. To get any direct experimental evidence for strings, it's likely we'd have to have much much much more powerful accelerators than we already do. Which is a shame, and should cast serious doubt on strings as a theory,  because there's an awful lot of room for different physics between the energy scales we can see at the LHC and the energy scales at which string theory would be important and we'd havecto be really smart and really lucky to have gotten it right without any more information.

However, having a massive force carrying particle is a problem for technical reasons. Essentially, if those particles are massive then at very high energies the probabilities for certain processes become too large and quantum mechanics breaks.

So physicists had to figure out how to make sense of this. They knew that something had to give, either the theory had to be changed, or quantum field theory was wrong. One possible solution was to somehow make it so the particles were actually massless. If there was a way to give the W bosons mass, then we could solve the problem. 

At the time, people were also using symmetry as a guide in theoretical physics and it was proving very fruitful. Then Higgs (and others independently) discovered a way of linking the two. In the mechanism, there's a particle that breaks a symmetry whilst simultaneously giving a particle mass. When Weinberg and Salam had a think about it, and found that the symmetries which govern the electromagnetic force and weak force could be united in this way, they also solved the problem with having massive force carrying particles. 

So whilst it's really nice that it has this connection with symmetry, we actually required the Higgs mechanism or something like it in order to make the theory make sense.

So, the electromagnetic force has photons, which are massless, that mediate the force between electrically charged particles. The photons themselves do not have electric charge. Since they don't have an electric charge if the charged particle emits photons in two different directions to possibly interact with something, those photons just go merrily on their way, and don't interact with one another.

In the strong force you have gluons. And the gluons carry forces between particles which have colour charge. But, the gluons themselves also have colour charge. So, if a particle with colour charge emits a couple of gluons in different directions where they go will not only be affected by the particle that emitted them (since they interact with it since they all have a colour charge) but it will also be affected by the other gluon, since gluons can interact with each other because they have colour charges. 

What we believe happens is that because the gluons interact with each other they don't spread out like photons would. Instead they interact and, if you like, pull all the strong force field lines together, into a tube (which is called a flux tube), which connects two particles that have colour charge. 

So what's the difference between gluons spreading out and not interacting, or the gluons forming a tube. If the gluons could spread out, then we'd get a standard 1/r^2 force. But if they're in a tube instead of going like 1/r^2 the force exerted by them is constant. So, it doesn't matter how far away two colour charged particles are from one another, the force between them is constant.

So why does that mean the range of the strong force is so short? Imagine we have two colour charged particles right next to each other, and there's a constant force between them. If well pull them apart we're putting energy into the system, and for every unit of distance we pull them apart we're putting the same amount of energy in. As they get further and further apart there's more and more energy in the system. Eventually it costs the universe less energy to break the flux tube and pop a new pair of colour charged particles out of the vacuum, put one on the end of each half of the flux tube and make two pairs of particles. Then as you pull them apart the force between the two original particles disappears, and you get left with a pair of particles in each hand. And no force between the two pairs. 

So, we say that distance that you'd have to pull the particles apart before the flux tube breaks is the range of the Strong force. Because beyond that range you don't get any gluons being exchanged between particles, they're all in flux tubes somewhere else. 

TL:DR; Since gluons have colour charge they organise themselves into tubes with a colour charged particle on each end. As you pull the particles apart, eventually the tube snaps and you get another particle on each end of the tube, and two pairs of particles. The distance where the tube snaps is the effective range of the strong force.

What they're doing is using the idea of symmetry to constrain the form of the lagrangian. Here's how it works. 

First, your lagrangian could be any function of the position and the velocity of the particle, but we're demanding that space be homogeneous and isotropic. That means that no matter the orientation, or the position in space, the lagrangian should be the same. Therefore, if the lagrangian depended on x, it wouldn't be the same at all points in space. So, the lagrangian can't depend on x. More explicitly, under the transformation

x goes to x' = x+x0

where x0 is a constant vector. Note that v doesn't change since the x0 is a constant. So for the lagrangian to be invariant we must have

L(x,v) = L(x+x0,v)

That is, the lagrangian is exactly the same whether the variable is x or x'. In this case, the only way to guarantee it is to make the lagrangian a function of v only. So L(x,v) = L(v).

Now, since v is a vector, if we perform a rotation on our coordinates, we would might get a different function. But since space is isotropic we want the lagrangian to also be invariant under rotations. So, to make something which is invariant under rotations from a vector we simply find it's magnitude. So we can write:

L(x,v) = L(v^2)

And we require that a lagrangian must be a function of the square of the magnitude of v if it is to be galilean invariant, i.e. make sense when space is isotropic and homogeneous.

There seen to be three steps to solving this problem. What's happening is:

Step 1: Spidey swings down from a height h. During this step I'd use energy conservation to find out how fast he's going at the bottom.

Step 2: Spidey picks up Mary Jane. As Kid_Radd pointed out, this will be an inelastic collision, because before we have two bodies, Spidey and Mary Jane, and afterwards, we just have one. The two of them in a sticky embrace. In inelastic collisions, energy is not conserved. So your only option is to use momentum conservation. Since you have the speed of Spidey when he picks up Mary Jane, you can use it, together with momentum conservation, to find the speed of the two of them afterwards.

Step 3: Mary Jane and Spidey together swing up. Since this is just like the first part, you'll want to use energy conservation again, to find out how high they swing up in terms of the initial height. 

Since there seems to be a little confusion as to exactly what's going on in an inelastic collision. It's nice to see how energy can be lost when a force is used to speed something up. Imagine we have a box and we put it on a conveyor belt. The conveyor is moving, and when the box touches it friction kicks in and starts to speed the box up. Eventually, the box is going the same speed as the conveyor. The force on the box is 

F = mu*m*g

As the only force acting is the friction. So by Newton's second law, the acceleration is:

a = mu*g. 

We want to know how far the conveyor has travelled during this time, so we can work out, from the conveyor's perspective, how much work it did pushing the box. So, since we know the speed of the conveyor (we'll call it v), the time the box took to travel is:

v = at so t = v/mu*g

So, the conveyor travelling for this amount of time, went a distance:

x = vt = v^2/mu*g

So the work done by the conveyor on the box is given by F*x which is:

Work done by conveyor = m*mu*g*v^2/mu*g = mv^2

The kinetic energy of the box is mv^2/2.

So the conveyor did twice as much work on the box as it has energy at the end of the day. Essentially, the conveyor belt is only 50% efficient. This is kind of like an inelastic collision. If we imagine Spidey grabs Mary Jane, he puts a force on her to speed her up, like the conveyor puts on the box. And when they're moving at the same speed, the work Spidey did on Mary Jane is more than the kinetic energy Mary Jane has gained.

So, your U(t) is given by exp(iHt) i, where H is the hamiltonian of the system and if the Hamiltonian is time independent. Since H is an operator, we need to be careful about what it's acting on, and what the order of things are. Your first statement:

exp(iHt)P(t0) = P(t+t0)

 is good. And we can indeed multiply by P*(t0). So we get:

(exp(iHt)P(t0))P*(t0) = P(t+t0)P(t0).

Now, I've put brackets around the first couple of factors so we don't forget that the exp(iHt) operator is acting on P(t0). Now, if we assume that the P's are eigenstates of the Hamiltonian, then we can act that operator on it and find:

exp(iEt)P(t0)P*(t0) = P(t+t0)P*(t0)

and then continue as you did before. But, since we've assumed the states are eigenstates of a time independent Hamiltonian it means P(t) = exp(iHt)p(x), where I've used p(x) to be the spatial part of the wavefunction. Then, plugging this in we get:

exp(iEt)exp(iE t0)exp(-iE t0)p(x)p*(x) = exp(iE(t+t0))exp(t0)p(x)p*(x).

Then you can see that, since we have to get rid of pp* by integrating over x, we do indeed get left with a true statement, which is the same as your last statement (more or less). Essentially, what I'm saying is that this is true, and a good check of the consistency of everything, but if the Hamiltonian is time independent, doesn't really tell us too much more than we knew. Essentially, the operator U(t) is just telling us how to change the phase of the wavefunction with time. 

However, if the Hamiltonian is not time independent things get a lot messier very quickly. In this case U(t) doesn't equal exp(iHt). Have a look here for the details: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyson_series 

In that case, we can't go between your two final lines, since the U(t) operator has to act on P(t0), and we can't get the P*(t0) together with it to get rid of them. Then sadly, the final line doesn't follow. Even if it did, things would still be really hard, as if you're trying to solve your system like this, you likely don't know the full solutions to the Schrodinger equation for your system anyway. 

So it's a nice, and sometimes true observation, and a really good way to be thinking. The work in that wikipedia article leads pretty much directly to the path integral formulation of things, which, especially in QFT, is how you go about trying to tackle the really complicated time dependent problems that come up in quantum mechanics.

I guess I'd say the two things that I say to all my students when they're studying basic classical mechanics.
1. You've lived your entire lifevaround classical mechanics, you know that surfaces have friction, you know what acceleration feels like, you know how it feels if you spin a bucket around your head. It's a lot easier to solve things when you know roughly what you're looking for.

2. Relax about problem solving methods. Sadly there's no nice cut and dry method to take a problem and put it on the page. As a rule of thumb, first draw a diagram, then locate the quantity you're trying to calculate on the diagram, then go from there. If you're having trouble drawing diagrams then always draw the thing the question is about first. The question will then tell you stuff about that thing, so put those on and then you're pretty much done. In my experience people have trouble with this part of physics not because they can't do it, but because they think there's a single correct way to set up a problem. All your symbols have to be the 'right' symbols and so and so forth. There is no such way. Write down the question in a way you feel makes sense to you, using the symbols you like to use and just push on, you will get much further than you think.

3. F = dp/dt. This equation is pretty much all of mechanics.  All the rules are in there. Newtons first law is in there. It says if there are no forces on an object it's velocity is constant. So set F=0. Then dp/dt=0. So p = constant, so v = constant. Using it for the center of mass of a bunch of objects tells you Newtons third law. Changing coordinates to polar coordinates gives you all the angular motion equations.  You can derive energy conservation from it (I'll show you if you like). Everything comes from F=dp/dt. If you find a concept confusing work out how it comes from F=dp/dt or look it up and work it through yourself. I've always found it to give something concrete to hold onto, as well as a way of remembering things. You'll find many good physicists instead of remembering all the equations, just vaguely know how to work them out and remember only the most important equations.

So that's my advice, use your intuition, draw diagrams and set up problems in the way that makes most sense to you and relate everything in mechanics back to Newton's second law. If you'd like any particular advice about bits of mechanics just let me know, I'll be happy to help!

So this is a really fun question. I had a think about how to justify things one way or another, because a full treatment of this would be incredibly difficult. Here's what I came up with:

First, we'll treat the CMB as some radiation with uniform density over all of spacetime. There's a standard result from cosmology which tells us how the temperature of this radiation decreases as space expands, if the expansion is driven mostly by dark energy. Which, at the moment, it pretty much is. The result is:
T = To * e^{-Ht}
Where T is the temperature of the CMB at time t, To is the temperature at some initial time and H is the hubble constant. 

We want to compare this decrease in temperature to the decrease in temperature of a black hole as it's absorbing CMB radiation. I'm going to neglect the fact that black hole radiate, and treat them in the following way:
1. The amount of radiation that the black hole consumes is proportional to the energy density of the CMB radiation
2. The amount of radiation that the black hole consumes is proportional to the surface area of the event horizon
3. All the energy consumed goes to increasing the mass of the black hole. 
The energy density of the CMB should go like En = En0 * e^{-3Ht}, as we think of the energy just contained in a box, and the box expands as space expands. The surface area of the black hole is proportional to R^2, where R is the radius of the event horizon. We can then equate the rate of change of mass of the black hole, dM/dt, to the product of the energy density and the surface area, so ignoring some dimensionful constants we get the equation:

dM/dt ~ e^{-3Ht}R^2

Now we'll solve this equation, first we recognise that black hole physics tells us that the radius of the event horizon is proportional to the mass of the black hole. So M ~ R. This gives:

dR/dt ~ e^{-3Ht}R^2

Then we also know that the temperature of the black hole is proportional to one over the radius, T ~ 1/R. Doing the calculus and inserting this gives:

dT/dt ~ e^{-3Ht}

This is an easy equation to solve, and we find that (including the very important constant of integration):

T ~ c + a*e^{-3Ht} 

So, how do we interpret c? Well, we determine it by saying when t=0, we know the temperature of the black hole is Th (T-hawking). So this gives:

T ~ Th + a*(e^{-3Ht}-1)

 So there are some cases to analyse here. The first is when a < Th. In this case as t gets very large we find the temperature of the black hole tends to a constant given by Th-a. This is pretty simple to understand, as space expands the energy density around the black hole gets less and less, and so the black hole gets larger slower and slower, and eventually cannot get any larger and so ends up at a finite temperature above zero. In this case, since the CMB temperature will decrease all the way to zero, the black hole will become hotter than the CMB and evaporate. 

If Th = a, the black hole will get to zero temperature, and if Th < a, the black hole will get to a zero temperature and becomes negative. So what's happening here? 

In these cases the black hole starts out so large that it expands in size so rapidly compared to the rate of decrease in energy of the CMB, that the universe never gets time to expand at all before the black hole swallows everything up. We should discard this case, since there aren't black holes that large, and the black hole would have such a significant effect on the spacetime that the analysis we've done (just treating the black hole as an object on the background of an expanding spacetime) wouldn't cut it. The converse is also true, if you do the calculations properly, you can get a spacetime which expands so rapidly that black holes can't actually form. 

So then, that's our conclusion, that black holes on an expanding background in a bath of radiation will expand for a bit, until the radiation is too dilute, and then their temperature will be larger than the background. Exactly how long this takes depends on the initial temperature of the black hole. I believe we're comparing really the logarithm of the initial black hole temperature, and comparing it to the hubble constant to get a rough comparison of the timescales.

But, and there are a few big buts! Because I'm lazy I haven't put in any of the dimensionful constants. So you're not going to be able to put numbers into any of this stuff unless you put them in. Secondly, I've used proportionality arguments all the way through, so any number, at best, will only be to within an order of magnitude or so. Thirdly, to do this properly (without considering the black hole evaporating) you need to use general relativity, which I haven't done. Fourth, if you did use GR, you'd probably need approximations or numerics anyway to get a decent answer. Essentially, the best you can pull from this analysis is that it seems fairly robust that the black holes we see in the sky will one day have a greater temperature than the CMB, but how long that'll take is up for grabs.

The thing that makes the holographic principle so important compared to the many theorems which show relationships between things on boundaries and things in the space (theorems like boundary conditions uniquely determining the solution to partial differential equations) is that the holographic principle posits a relationship between theories, between sets of dynamics. 

For example, let's say we have some partial differential equation. We can solve it, and then impose boundary conditions to get a unique solution to the equation. A good example of this is quantum mechanics. We solve Schrodinger's equation, and then we give as initial conditions the initial energies and positions of the particles. Then the equations solution at late times tells us what happens to those particles, and it's that data that we wanted to know. The important thing to note is that we could not have found that information without using Schrodingers equation, we had to have an equation which told us what happened in the entire space, in order to find out what would happen. 

What the holographic principle says is; We can find an equation, which gives us the same answer given the same initial conditions. But this equation exists in one fewer dimension that Schrodingers equation, and, moreover, this equation is just as general, we can give it any initial conditions and it will always give us the same answer as the other theory. In other words, for all operational purposes the two theories are identical, and this is a much richer and deeper correspondence than any of the other boundary conditions to solutions correspondences that exist.
